steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting Sophia, a light-weight second-order optimizer meant to make LLM pre-training faster than with Adam.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLM pre-training is expensive; efficiency is the bottleneck
- Adam dominates; why faster optimizers are hard to design
- Sophia: what it is and headline results
- How Sophia works (Hessian estimators, EMA, clipping) and ease of integration
- Why it works: heterogeneous curvature, clipping as a safeguard
- Theory

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Cost of pre-training
  - LLM capabilities grow with scale
  - pre-training very slow: massive data + model sizes, hundreds of thousands of updates
  - PaLM: two months on 6144 TPUs, 10 million dollars
  - goal: faster optimizer -> same loss for less time/cost, or better loss for same budget
- Adam and the difficulty
  - Adam (+ variants) dominant for GPT, OPT, Gopher, LLAMA
  - benefit of Adam's first-order pre-conditioner not well understood
  - only light-weight pre-conditioners affordable; overhead must be offset by fewer iterations
  - K-FAC block-diagonal Hessian: expensive for LLMs
  - prior work: automated search over light-weight gradient-based pre-conditioners -> Lion; faster on vision Transformers, diffusion models, limited on LLMs
- Sophia
  - Second-order Clipped Stochastic Optimization
  - cheap stochastic estimate of diagonal Hessian as pre-conditioner + clipping for worst-case update size
  - GPT-2: same validation loss with 50 \% fewer steps than Adam
  - same memory / time per step -> 50 \% less compute and wall-clock (Figure 1 (a)&(b))
  - comparing run-time to reach same loss is correct comparison (Section 3.2)
  - scaling 125M to 770M favours Sophia; gap at 100K steps grows with size (Figure 1 (c))
  - 540M Sophia = 770M Adam; latter needs 40% more training time and inference cost
- Mechanics
  - diagonal Hessian estimated on a mini-batch every k step, k=10
  - (a) unbiased Hessian-vector product estimator; (b) biased estimator via mini-batch gradient with resampled labels
  - both 5% overhead per step on average
  - update = EMA of gradient / EMA of diagonal Hessian, clipped by a scalar; element-wise; Algorithm 3
  - no special model architecture/infrastructure; works with PyTorch, JAX
- Why it works
  - adapts to heterogeneous curvature across dimensions (instability/slowdown in LLM losses)
  - penalizes sharp dimensions more than flat ones -> uniform loss decrease; Adam's updates uniform -> slow in flat dims (Section 2.1)
  - clipping guards against inaccurate Hessian estimates, fast Hessian change, non-convexity (Newton -> maxima/saddles)
  - allows infrequent (k=10) stochastic Hessian; prior second-order methods update every step
- Theory
  - simplified Sophia on convex functions
  - runtime bound independent of local condition number and worst-case curvature

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Language models (LLMs) gain phenomenal capabilities as their scale grows. But pre-training LLMs takes an incredible amount of time because of the massive datasets and model sizes, and hundreds of thousands of updates to the model parameters are needed. For example, PaLM was trained for two months on 6144 TPUs, which cost 10 million dollars.

So pre-training efficiency is a major bottleneck for scaling up LLMs. In this work we want to improve pre-training efficiency with a faster optimizer, which either reduces the time and cost needed to reach the same pre-training loss, or gets a better pre-training loss with the same budget.

Adam (or its variants) is the optimizer that is mostly used for training LLMs, such as GPT, OPT, Gopher and LLAMA. It is challenging to design faster optimizers for LLMs. First, the benefit of the first-order (gradient-based) pre-conditioner in Adam is not well understood yet. Second, we are constrained in which pre-conditioners we can choose, because we can only afford light-weight ones whose overhead is offset by the speed-up in the number of iterations. For example, the block-diagonal Hessian pre-conditioner in K-FAC is expensive for LLMs. On the other hand, prior work automatically searched among light-weight gradient-based pre-conditioners and found Lion, which is a lot faster than Adam on vision Transformers and diffusion models but only gets a limited speed-up on LLMs.

In this paper we introduce Sophia, Second-order Clipped Stochastic Optimization, which is a light-weight second-order optimizer. It uses a cheap stochastic estimate of the diagonal of the Hessian as a pre-conditioner, and a clipping mechanism to control the worst-case update size. When pre-training language models like GPT-2, Sophia gets the same validation pre-training loss as Adam with 50 \% fewer steps. Sophia keeps almost the same memory and average time per step, so the speedup also means 50 \% less total compute and 50 \% less wall-clock time (See Figure 1 (a)&(b)). We also note that comparing the run-time needed to reach the same loss is a correct way to compare optimizer speed for LLMs; see Section 3.2 for more details.

Also, the scaling law based on model size from 125M to 770M favours Sophia over Adam, and the gap between Sophia and Adam with 100K steps gets bigger as the model size increases (Figure 1 (c)). In particular, Sophia on a 540M-parameter model with 100K steps gives the same validation loss as Adam on a 770M-parameter model with 100K steps. The latter model needs 40% more training time and 40% more inference cost.

- Mechanics
  - diagonal Hessian estimated on a mini-batch every k step, k=10
  - (a) unbiased Hessian-vector product estimator; (b) biased estimator, mini-batch gradient with resampled labels; both 5% overhead per step
  - update = EMA of gradient / EMA of diagonal Hessian, clipped by a scalar; element-wise; Algorithm 3
  - easy to integrate; only needs mini-batch gradients or Hessian-vector products (PyTorch, JAX)
- Why it works
  - adapts to heterogeneous curvature; penalizes sharp dims more than flat ones; Adam uniform -> slow in flat dims (Section 2.1)
  - clipping: safeguard vs inaccurate/fast-changing Hessian, non-convexity; allows Hessian every k=10 step; prior methods every step
- Theory
  - simplified versions on convex functions; bound independent of local condition number and worst-case curvature

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Language models (LLMs) gain phenomenal capabilities as their scale grows. But pre-training LLMs takes an incredible amount of time because of the massive datasets and model sizes, and hundreds of thousands of updates to the model parameters are needed. For example, PaLM was trained for two months on 6144 TPUs, which cost 10 million dollars.

So pre-training efficiency is a major bottleneck for scaling up LLMs. In this work we want to improve pre-training efficiency with a faster optimizer, which either reduces the time and cost needed to reach the same pre-training loss, or gets a better pre-training loss with the same budget.

Adam (or its variants) is the optimizer that is mostly used for training LLMs, such as GPT, OPT, Gopher and LLAMA. It is challenging to design faster optimizers for LLMs. First, the benefit of the first-order (gradient-based) pre-conditioner in Adam is not well understood yet. Second, we are constrained in which pre-conditioners we can choose, because we can only afford light-weight ones whose overhead is offset by the speed-up in the number of iterations. For example, the block-diagonal Hessian pre-conditioner in K-FAC is expensive for LLMs. On the other hand, prior work automatically searched among light-weight gradient-based pre-conditioners and found Lion, which is a lot faster than Adam on vision Transformers and diffusion models but only gets a limited speed-up on LLMs.

In this paper we introduce Sophia, Second-order Clipped Stochastic Optimization, which is a light-weight second-order optimizer. It uses a cheap stochastic estimate of the diagonal of the Hessian as a pre-conditioner, and a clipping mechanism to control the worst-case update size. When pre-training language models like GPT-2, Sophia gets the same validation pre-training loss as Adam with 50 \% fewer steps. Sophia keeps almost the same memory and average time per step, so the speedup also means 50 \% less total compute and 50 \% less wall-clock time (See Figure 1 (a)&(b)). We also note that comparing the run-time needed to reach the same loss is a correct way to compare optimizer speed for LLMs; see Section 3.2 for more details.

Also, the scaling law based on model size from 125M to 770M favours Sophia over Adam, and the gap between Sophia and Adam with 100K steps gets bigger as the model size increases (Figure 1 (c)). In particular, Sophia on a 540M-parameter model with 100K steps gives the same validation loss as Adam on a 770M-parameter model with 100K steps. The latter model needs 40% more training time and 40% more inference cost.

Concretely, Sophia estimates the diagonal entries of the Hessian of the loss using a mini-batch of examples every k step (k=10 in our implementation). We consider two options for the diagonal Hessian estimator: (a) an unbiased estimator that uses a Hessian-vector product, with the same run-time as a mini-batch gradient up to a constant factor, and (b) a biased estimator that uses one mini-batch gradient computed with resampled labels. Both estimators only add 5% overhead per step (on average). At every step, Sophia updates the parameter with an exponential moving average (EMA) of the gradient divided by the EMA of the diagonal Hessian estimate, and then this is clipped by a scalar. (All operations are element-wise.) The pseudo-code is in Algorithm 3.

Sophia can also be easily integrated into existing training pipelines, and it does not have special requirements on the model architecture or the computing infrastructure. With either Hessian estimator, Sophia only needs standard mini-batch gradients or Hessian-vector products, which are supported in auto-differentiation frameworks like PyTorch and JAX.

Because of the Hessian-based pre-conditioner, Sophia adapts better than Adam to the heterogeneous curvatures in different parameter dimensions, which often happen in the landscape of LLM losses and cause instability or slowdown. Sophia's pre-conditioner is more aggressive than Adam's. Sophia penalizes updates in sharp dimensions (where the Hessian is large) more strongly than in flat dimensions (where the Hessian is small), so the loss decreases uniformly across all parameter dimensions. Adam's updates on the other hand are mostly uniform across all parameter dimensions, which means the loss decreases more slowly in flat dimensions. (See Section 2.1 for more discussion.) Because of this Sophia converges in fewer iterations. And because the diagonal Hessian estimate is light-weight, the speed-up in the number of steps becomes a speed-up in total compute and wall-clock time.

The clipping mechanism in Sophia controls the worst-case size of the updates in all directions. This protects against the negative effect of inaccurate Hessian estimates, fast changes of the Hessian over time, and the non-convex landscape (where the vanilla Newton's method may converge to local maxima or saddle points and not local minima). Because of this safeguard we can estimate the Hessian infrequently (every k=10 step) and stochastically. Prior second-order methods on the other hand often update the Hessian estimates every step.

We give theoretical analyses of much simplified versions of Sophia on convex functions. The runtime bound does not depend on the local condition number (the ratio between maximum and minimum curvature at the local minimum) or the worst-case curvature (that is, the smoothness parameter), which shows the advantage of Sophia in adapting to heterogeneous curvatures across parameter dimensions.

steps.text:

However, pre-training LLMs is incredibly time-consuming because of the massive datasets and model sizes—hundreds of thousands of updates to the model parameters are required. For example, PaLM was trained for two months on 6144 TPUs, which cost 10 million dollars [7].

Pre-training efficiency is thus a major bottleneck in scaling up LLMs. This work aims to improve pre-training efficiency with a faster optimizer, which either reduces the time and cost to reach the same pre-training loss, or achieves a better pre-training loss with the same budget.

Adam [8] (or its variants [9,10,11]) is the dominant optimizer for training LLMs, such as GPT [1,3], OPT [4], Gopher [12] and LLAMA [5]. Designing faster optimizers for LLMs is challenging. First, the benefit of the first-order (gradient-based) pre-conditioner in Adam is not yet well understood [13,14,15]. Second, the choice of pre-conditioners is constrained because we can only afford light-weight options whose overhead can be offset by the speed-up in the number of iterations. For example, the block-diagonal Hessian pre-conditioner in K-FAC is expensive for LLMs [16,17,18,19]. On the other hand, [20] automatically search among light-weight gradient-based pre-conditioners and identify Lion, which is substantially faster than Adam on vision Transformers and diffusion models but achieves only limited speed-up on LLMs [20].

This paper introduces Sophia, Second-order Clipped Stochastic Optimization, a light-weight second-order optimizer that uses an inexpensive stochastic estimate of the diagonal of the Hessian as a pre-conditioner and a clipping mechanism to control the worst-case update size. On pre-training language models such as GPT-2, Sophia achieves the same validation pre-training loss as Adam with 50 \% fewer steps. Because Sophia keeps almost the same memory and average time per step, the speedup also translates to 50 \% less total compute and 50 \% less wall-clock time (See Figure 1 (a)&(b)). We also note that comparing the run-time to reach the same loss is a correct way to compare the speed of optimizers for LLMs; see Section 3.2 for more details.

Moreover, the scaling law based on model size from 125M to 770M favours Sophia over Adam—the gap between Sophia and Adam with 100K steps increases as the model size increases (Figure 1 (c)). In particular, Sophia on a 540M-parameter model with 100K steps gives the same validation loss as Adam on a 770M-parameter model with 100K steps. Note that the latter model needs 40% more training time and 40% more inference cost.

Concretely, Sophia estimates the diagonal entries of the Hessian of the loss using a mini-batch of examples every k step (with k=10 in our implementation). We consider two options for diagonal Hessian estimators: (a) an unbiased estimator that uses a Hessian-vector product with the same run-time as a mini-batch gradient up to a constant factor, and (b) a biased estimator that uses one mini-batch gradient calculated with resampled labels. Both estimators only introduce 5% overhead per step (on average). At every step, Sophia updates the parameter with an exponential moving average (EMA) of the gradient divided by the EMA of the diagonal Hessian estimate, then clipped by a scalar. (All operations are element-wise.) See Algorithm 3 for the pseudo-code.

Additionally, Sophia can be seamlessly integrated into existing training pipelines, without special requirements on the model architecture or computing infrastructure. With either of the Hessian estimators, Sophia only requires standard mini-batch gradients or Hessian-vector products, which are supported in auto-differentiation frameworks such as PyTorch [21] and JAX [22].

Thanks to the Hessian-based pre-conditioner, Sophia adapts more efficiently than Adam to the heterogeneous curvatures in different parameter dimensions, which often occur in the landscape of LLM losses and cause instability or slowdown. Sophia has a more aggressive pre-conditioner than Adam—it applies a stronger penalization to updates in sharp dimensions (where the Hessian is large) than in flat dimensions (where the Hessian is small), ensuring a uniform loss decrease across all parameter dimensions. In contrast, Adam's updates are mostly uniform across all parameter dimensions, leading to a slower loss decrease in flat dimensions. (See Section 2.1 for more discussion.) This makes Sophia converge in fewer iterations. Thanks to the light-weight diagonal Hessian estimate, the speed-up in the number of steps translates to a speed-up in total compute and wall-clock time.

Sophia's clipping mechanism controls the worst-case size of the updates in all directions, safeguarding against the negative impact of inaccurate Hessian estimates, rapid Hessian changes over time, and the non-convex landscape (where the vanilla Newton's method may converge to local maxima or saddle points instead of local minima). The safeguard allows us to estimate the Hessian infrequently (every k=10 step) and stochastically. In contrast, prior second-order methods often update Hessian estimates every step [16,17,23,24].

We provide theoretical analyses of much simplified versions of Sophia on convex functions. The runtime bound depends neither on the local condition number (the ratio between maximum and minimum curvature at the local minimum) nor on the worst-case curvature (that is, the smoothness parameter), demonstrating the advantage of Sophia in adapting to heterogeneous curvatures across parameter dimensions.
